quote: Attitude polarization. Exposing subjects to an apparently balanced set of pro and con arguments will exaggerate their initial polarization.
content: Taber & Lodge (2006) is influential, and several of its effects (prior-attitude, disconfirmation) are reasonably robust. But "attitude polarization," the idea that balanced arguments push people further apart, has not held up well. The original demonstration (Lord, Ross & Lepper 1979) was small, and replications find polarization weak and inconsistent (Kuhn & Lao 1996). Its dramatic cousin, the "backfire effect" (corrections strengthening false beliefs), largely failed to replicate: Wood & Porter (2019), across 52 issues and over 10,000 subjects, found corrections overwhelmingly move people toward accuracy. The bias is real; the backfire framing is mostly a myth.

quote: If you’re irrational to start with, having more knowledge can hurt you.
content: The "sophistication effect," that the politically knowledgeable are more biased, is the hook of the essay, but it rests on a single pair of studies (two issues, gun control and affirmative action) and the picture since is mixed. Kahan et al.'s (2017) motivated-numeracy work finds high-numeracy subjects can be more polarized on identity-relevant issues, supporting the idea; but on most questions expertise improves accuracy and reduces bias. Whether knowledge nets out as harmful depends heavily on whether the topic is identity-protective, a contingency the blanket claim "having more knowledge can hurt you" papers over.
